item.title: Reading as a Green Flag Is a Dating Trend
item.description:
Mating

Reading as a Green Flag Is a Dating Trend

What people read can help you better read them.

Posted November 13, 2026

Key points
  • Reading has become a prominent "green flag" that people are actively looking for on dating profiles.
  • People's reading habits can end up being a whole lot more important than their physical appearances.
  • Reading can say a lot about a person's intellectual curiosity, perspectives, interests, and adaptability.
  • To meet people, consider social events that focus on reading such as book clubs and "romantasy" ones.
There seems to be a reading divide in the U.S., between those who regularly read books and those hardly read them at all
Source: Adrien from Pexels

Are you looking to date someone who's on the same page with you? Or how about on any page—as in, does the person actually read things like books and not just social media posts? Well, you may have read about how reading has become a prominent green flag—meaning that many people are actively looking for it on dating profiles and dates.

For example, after pop star Dua Lipa married actor Callum Turner, many fans seemed to get excited about the cover version, so to speak, of their meet-cute, as described by an article by Ellen Durney for Buzzfeed. Turner indicated that they had first met at a mutual friend’s birthday party and soon realized that they were both reading the book Trust by Hernán Díaz and were even on the same chapter. This apparently helped them trust each other more, with Turner claiming that he had told Lipa then, “So we’re on the same page.” And that, kids, is how Dua became a duo.

How Reading Can Be a Green Flag

These days, whether someone reads, period, can be a dating screening criterion, depending on where you stand on this whole reading thing. That's because there is a big reading divide in the U.S. For example, the Pew Research Center found that nearly a quarter (~23%) of Americans surveyed didn't even touch a book over the past 12 months. In fact, the National Endowment for the Arts and American Time Use Survey have shown that only 16% or so of Americans may be reading on a daily basis, and over 51% may be reading absolutely no books each year.

Social media may be making this divide more obvious. Just look at how many times someone posts an opinion and the response is something like "Have you even read about this?" or even "Did you even read the link that you posted?" So, if you do fall on the regularly reading side of the divide, it might make sense to have regular reading as a minimal dating requirement.

Reading in Itself Can Be Attractive

But it could go even beyond that. The reading app Headway found in a survey that ”Some 24% of people instantly swipe right on dating profiles that show someone reading, while 75% prefer a partner who is well-read over someone physically attractive." Yep, reading could even be, gasp, sexy. That might have been a War and Peace of news to you in high school, when it seemed like all that people were interested in was looks.

But if you think about it, regularly reading stuff that's more than just cereal boxes and messages with ROFL in them can tell a lot about a person. It could suggest that the person is intellectually curious, willing to learn, and more thoughtful and mindful. There is also the standard saying that the brain is the biggest and most powerful sexual organ. The size of a person's creativity, empathy, and knowledge could play a bigger role in pleasing a partner than the size of anything else. And if you are looking for, umm, enhancement in all those areas, reading can be at your service.

What People Specifically Read Can Say a Lot About Them

Once you find someone who actually reads regularly—assuming that's what you want, since you have already gotten this far on this article—it can also help to find out what, specifically, the person reads. What someone reads can tell you a whole lot more about a person than the person's photo. That's because reading is something that takes time and effort and is done on one's own time.

So, those who will dedicate their time to reading about something are likely interested in that thing at least to some degree. For example, anyone who has read a lot of books about cats probably likes cats. Or, maybe, is preparing for the big cat government overthrow that will eventually occur. Either way, that person likely has a more informed opinion about cats.

Someone's reading materials can also be a clue to that person's point of view. Guess what reading "Surrounded by Idiots" may say about a person's current life situation. Also, the diversity of their reading materials could reflect their diversity of thought and perspectives and their open-mindedness.

All of this can be important information since a big part of dating is finding the right match in terms of personality, values, and other core qualities. A person's reading list doesn't necessarily say everything about someone. For example, when I was doing research to write an article about farts, I was reading a lot about farts. But I am more than farts. Nevertheless, reading lists can be another clue to help you read someone better.

There's Been an Increase in Social Events That Revolve Around Reading

Eventbrite data have showed significant increases in the number of "romantasy" events such as this.
Source: Courtesy of Fabled Fantasy Events; photography by Pixie Vision Photography

There's a lot to be read about using reading to help gauge people, but also, to meet people in the first place. Eventbrite data did show a 33% increase in book club events in the first half of 2026. Such data also showed that the number "romantasy" events around the U.S. have gone up by 196% in 2026 compared to 2025, with attendance jumping by 237%. A "romantasy event" is a gathering that's built around the whole romantic fantasy literary genre. This is fiction that brings together mystical worlds and romantic plots.

For example, there was the three-day Romantasy BookCon in Orlando, Florida, in October. There was cosplay, author appearances, and book signings, and a variety of ways lovers of this genre could mix together. Now, while the focus of that event was not dating, who knows what can happen when lovers of the same thing come together. They might end up becoming lovers of lovers of that thing.

All of this does not mean that you should pretend to like reading when you don't. People trying to be what they are not is a big reason why there are so many mismatches and bad relationships out there. But it does mean that if you do things by the book regularly, this could end up being the book on love for you.

item.title: Why We Love Talking Animals
item.description:
Anthropomorphism

Why We Love Talking Animals

Animals as mirrors of human nature.

Posted November 13, 2026

Key points
  • Across cultures and centuries, humans have told stories through animals.
  • Animals mirror our faults without making us defensive.
  • Animal fables can disguise satire and reveal universal truths.
Source: Neel Burton, AI-generated image.

From Aesop to Orwell, from the Three Little Pigs to Bugs Bunny, our stories are full of talking animals. Foxes flatter, lions boast, and donkeys mope. For thousands of years, we have used animals to tell stories about ourselves.

But why use animals? Why not just use people?

Consider this short tale by the ancient Greek fabulist Aesop, The Fox and the Mask:

A fox broke into the house of an actor and noticed a mask in the midst of a pile of stage accessories. The fox dragged out the mask and nuzzled and swatted it for a few moments, before saying, “What a handsome face, pity he has no brains.”

Or consider this fable from the Ancient Indian Panchatantra, in which a rabbit outwits a lion:

A lion was terrorising the animals of the jungle, killing far more than he could eat. To appease him, the animals agreed that, each day, they would send him one of their number. When a rabbit’s turn came, he arrived late, telling the lion that another lion had kept him by claiming to be the true king of the jungle. Enraged, the lion demanded to see this imposter. The rabbit led him to a well, in which the lion saw his own reflection. Mistaking it for his rival, he leapt in and drowned.

Animals as Mirrors

The use of animals creates new and striking possibilities. It stokes the imagination, making the tale seem more original and entertaining, even charming, without which it might fall flat as moralising or patronising. We are more willing to listen to a fox than to a preacher, and more likely to remember what it has to say.

The use of animals also enables the storyteller to isolate a vice and caricature it, while at the same time providing a fresh perspective on it. Each animal becomes a shorthand for a particular human vice or trait. We are often resistant to criticism, especially when it concerns our character. But when we laugh at a vain crow or a pessimistic donkey, we may be laughing at ourselves. The animal creates a certain psychological distance, enabling us to recognise our faults without feeling accused and becoming defensive.

On a deeper level, talking animals create a continuum between human and animal, revealing us as part of nature and at one with it, while also highlighting what sets us apart from the rest of creation, namely, speech and reason (Greek, logos) and the capacity for moral reflection.

From Fables and Fairy Tales to Political Satire

As I discuss in The Meaning of Myth, animals appeal especially to children, possibly because blurring the lines between human and animal is a form of pre-logical, magical thinking. Children readily attribute thoughts, feelings, and intentions to animals, and may find a talking rabbit or bear no more extraordinary than a talking human. For adults, the attraction is more subtle: the talking animal offers both an escape from reality and a means of understanding it, in particular, through the pleasure of analogising.

Finally, the use of animals can serve as a cover, a means of escaping censorship, or of generalising or universalising. Jean de La Fontaine (d. 1695) used the fable form to satirise French society, and George Orwell used it to satirise communism and other forms of totalitarianism, while also making us smile.

Animals delight us still today, every day, if only in cartoons and viral videos, because, as the fabulist might say, “So it is with men, too.”

You may also enjoy my companion piece, The Symbolism of Snakes.

item.title: Why One Good Thing Leads to Another
item.description:
Relationships

Why One Good Thing Leads to Another

Small actions lead to unexpected possibilities.

Posted November 13, 2026

The Toll Booth Surprise
Source: Flickr

After reading the responses to my last post about the art of asking questions, in which I described the importance of becoming better listeners to ensure more meaningful connection with others, I’ve been thinking about something else: how one small action can set other good things in motion.

Here’s what got me thinking. A woman from a media company that uses puppets to teach elementary-school children important skills reached out. She was so excited about the idea of teaching genuine curiosity to young people that she is talking with her staff about creating episodes on asking interesting questions.

She wrote: I'm part of the team behind Sunnyside Roadshow, a daily, five-minute social-emotional learning program for elementary school children that uses puppetry, storytelling, and humor to help develop important life skills.

"As I read your article, I found myself wondering: Can we begin teaching children, at an early age, the art of being genuinely curious about other people? Kids are naturally eager to share their own experiences, and understandably so! But could we help them learn to pause, listen, ask another question, and show interest in what someone else is saying?

…Rather than simply teaching children not to interrupt and act on impulse, what if we could help them discover the joy of being genuinely interested in another person's experiences? Could we intentionally model curiosity through our characters' conversations, showing children how asking one thoughtful follow-up question can make someone feel heard and valued? If they worked on these skills together in the classroom, wouldn't we help raise more thoughtful humans?"

Think about that.

A post about ways to deepen conversation through becoming better listeners might lead to children learning how to show interest in others. Those children could bring that curiosity to their friendships, their families, and eventually their adult relationships. We have no way of knowing how far those ripples might travel.

Other people wrote that the post prompted them to reflect on their own conversational habits. They recognized themselves in the tendency to tell stories and talk about themselves rather than ask questions, and vowed to be more inquisitive.

That’s how it starts. Someone does something. Someone else responds. And on and on.

And it doesn’t require writing a post or creating a children’s program.

Think about the times you checked out at Trader Joe’s and were asked, “What are your plans for today?” or “Got anything fun planned this weekend?” For some customers, that might be the only conversation they have all day. What seems like a casual question can be a moment of genuine connection. And think about the difference that brief connection might make—not only for the person leaving the store, but also for the people they encounter throughout the day.

A few months ago, as I was checking out of Trader Joe’s, a clerk asked me about my plans, and I mentioned that I was having a party.

“Any occasion?” he asked.

“Yes, my birthday.”

“Wait right here.”

He ran off and returned with a gorgeous bouquet of flowers—all my favorite colors. He had no idea how much that unexpected kindness meant to me. And now, months later, I’m telling you about it. His gesture is still traveling.

My mother understood something about this, too. A New Yorker, she would often pay the toll for a complete stranger in the car behind her when crossing the George Washington Bridge.

Imagine pulling up to the tollbooth, reaching for your money, and being told that someone had already paid. Someone you didn’t know and probably would never meet. I loved that about her.

Did those drivers go on to do something kind for someone else? I don’t know. But my mother’s gestures stayed with me. That, too, is a ripple.

We often think that making a difference requires a grand plan, lots of time, or something extraordinary to offer. Meanwhile, we overlook the opportunities right in front of us: asking a question and truly listening to the answer, offering a sincere compliment, including someone who seems left out, or letting someone know that something they did mattered.

So here’s my challenge: Do one small thing today that might set other good things in motion.

Treat it as an experiment. Notice what happens—to the other person and to you. You may see an immediate response, or you may never know where your gesture leads.

Either way, tip over that first domino. And watch the fun begin.

And if the spirit moves you, email me and tell me what happened. I’d love to hear.
